title: Letter Writing (Patra Lekhan)
tagline: One letter from a choice of two subjects: the assessed layout, the two registers, and content that answers the purpose.

sourceNote.boardprep: All notes, model openings, practice passages, vocabulary, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written against the CISCE ICSE Examination Year 2028 second-language syllabus registered for this subject. The names, addresses and institutions used in the models are fictional, and the practice passage is BoardPrep’s own writing rather than any prescribed or previously used text.

overview.intro: The syllabus records the letter task in the same open spirit as the composition: you write one letter from a choice of two subjects, suggestions may be provided, and the elements named as assessed are address, introduction, conclusion and layout. No letter subjects are prescribed, which means the format itself is what can be prepared — a frame that works for any subject, from an application for leave to a letter to a friend. This chapter builds that frame part by part: the order of the parts on the page, the register that a formal letter must hold from salutation to close, the warmth an informal letter may use without losing shape, and the development that turns a purpose into three clear paragraphs. It ends with the checklist of faults that most often betray an otherwise well-written letter, because layout is named as assessed and layout is the cheapest thing on the page to get right.

learningOutcomes: Restate what the syllabus statement records about the letter task and its assessed elements.
Lay out a formal letter in the correct order of parts, from address to signature.
Distinguish the formal and informal registers in tone, opening, body and close, with examples.
Develop the body of a letter so that purpose, details and courteous close are all present.
Recognise and correct the common layout and register faults before submitting a letter.

learn.title: What the syllabus records, and what is assessed

blocks.text: The syllabus statement for this task is short and worth knowing almost word for word: one letter is written from a choice of two subjects, suggestions may be provided with the subjects, and the elements named as assessed are the address, the introduction, the conclusion and the layout. Read carefully what that list contains — it is the frame of the letter rather than its style. Nobody is being asked to be witty or ornamental; the reader is being shown that the letter has a sender and a destination, a stated purpose, a completed close, and parts arranged in the order a reader expects to find them. That is good news for preparation: with no prescribed subjects, the format is the entire reusable content of this task, and the format can be practised until it is automatic.

blocks.caption: The assessed elements and what each one consists of
rows: Where the letter comes from and, in formal letters, whom it is going to
Let a reader identify both sides of the correspondence at a glance
The opening paragraph, after the salutation and subject
State the purpose within the first two or three sentences
The final paragraph of the body
Close the purpose politely as a request, thanks or news — without new material
The order and spacing of every part on the page
Put each part where the reader expects it, so the letter can be navigated

learn.title: The order of parts on the page

items: Sender’s address — at the top, in brief: house number, street, city, so a reply can find you.
Date — below the address, written plainly, because requests and applications often depend on it.
Receiver’s address and salutation — in a formal letter, the office or person and the respect the relationship requires.
Subject line — formal letters only: one line naming the purpose before the body begins.
Body — introduction first, then the details or request in ordered paragraphs, then the courteous close.
Subscription and signature — the leave-taking formula matched to the relationship, with the writer’s name below it.

blocks.text: Layout is assessed, and layout is simply this order kept honestly on the page. Each part has one job, and the reader navigates by it: the address locates the writer, the date fixes the occasion, the subject announces the purpose, the body develops it, and the subscription closes the exchange with a formula that tells the reader what kind of relationship this is. Two habits spoil the frame even when the sentences are good: beginning the body at the top of the page as though the letter were an essay, and appending the address and date afterwards, where they look like an afterthought. Write the frame in order, from the first line down, and the letter will read as a letter before a single argument in it has been judged.

learn.title: Formal letters: purpose first, register throughout

blocks.text: A formal letter is written to an official, an institution or an organisation, and its qualities follow from that: polite, brief and businesslike. The purpose belongs in the first sentence of the body — or in the subject line above it — because a formal reader is looking for the reason for writing before anything else. Details follow in order, with dates, numbers and names made precise enough to act on, and the close repeats the purpose as a request or an acknowledgment rather than introducing a new point. Since the syllabus prescribes no subjects, practise the situations this level commonly works with — a letter to the Principal about leave, a certificate or a fee concern, a letter to an editor or an official — not as a list of topics to memorise, but as rehearsals of one frame under different content.

items.text: Formal opening: “I am writing to request three days’ leave from 14 October, as my sister’s wedding keeps me away from school.”
items.note: Purpose, subject and reason in one sentence — the reader can act on the letter before reaching the second paragraph.

items.text: Formal close: “I shall be grateful if the leave is granted for the dates mentioned. Thanking you in advance.”
items.note: A courteous close that repeats the request as a request and completes the letter without adding new material.

learn.title: Informal letters: warmth without losing shape

blocks.text: An informal letter goes to a friend, a relative or an acquaintance, and its register changes without its structure changing. The greeting is personal, the opening is a natural remark about the person or the occasion, and the body moves through news, feelings and enquiries in whatever order the relationship takes them — yet the same assessed elements are present: an address and date, an introduction that says why you are writing, a development with specific detail, and a conclusion that completes the exchange. Warmth is not the same as shapelessness. A letter to a friend that never asks anything, never reports anything specific and never closes its thought is not informal; it is unfinished, and the friend reading it has been given mood rather than news.

items: Greeting: personal and matched to the relationship — a name, not an office.
Opening: a genuine first remark — an enquiry, an occasion, a shared memory — that leads into the reason for writing.
Body: news with specifics — what happened, when, what you thought — and at least one enquiry about the reader’s life.
Close: a warm leave-taking that completes the letter, followed by the subscription formula the relationship calls for.

learn.title: Building the body: purpose, detail, close

blocks.text: The body of a letter is three moves in order. The introduction states the purpose completely — who is writing, why, and what is being asked or said — so that a reader who reads only the first paragraph has the essentials. The middle develops that purpose: in a formal letter, the details, dates and facts that make the request actionable; in an informal one, the incidents, observations and feelings that make the news worth reading. The conclusion closes the purpose politely — repeating a request as a request, thanking, or wishing — and stops. What damages a body is not lack of material but lack of order: details that arrive before the purpose, a request buried in the third paragraph, a conclusion that raises a second subject just as the reader is leaving.

items.meaning: The one-line statement of purpose in a formal letter, placed between the salutation and the opening paragraph.
The form of address that opens the letter — respected or sir in formal use, a name in informal.
The closing unit: the leave-taking formula matched to the relationship, with the signature below it.
What the letter must achieve; it belongs in the first paragraph and is repeated in the close.

learn.title: The faults that most often cost this task

items: Wrong order of parts: address, date and salutation rearranged so the reader hunts for the sender or the purpose.
No subject line in a formal letter, leaving the body to announce its own reason for arriving.
Register mixed across the letter: a chatty opening in an application, or a stiff formulaic greeting to a friend.
Purpose late or missing: details and background before the reader knows what is being asked.
No conclusion: the letter stops at its last fact instead of closing the purpose courteously.
Subscription mismatched to the relationship — the formula that contradicts the tone of everything above it.

blocks.text: Every one of these faults is visible in a final read, which is why the checklist belongs to the last minutes rather than to writing time. Read the letter as its recipient will: first the frame — is every part in its expected place — then the first paragraph — is the purpose immediately clear — then the close — does it complete rather than continue. Then check the formula at the foot against the addressee, and the dates and names against reality. Practice makes the frame automatic: write the same letter twice a week under a self-set limit, once in each register, and audit the result against this list by name. Layout was named as assessed in the syllabus statement itself, and layout is the one part of this task that never depends on inspiration.

figures.caption: Figure: the order of parts in a letter
figures.description: A page-shaped vertical diagram with six stacked bands, each labelled with the part that belongs there: sender’s address at the top, then the date, then the receiver’s address and salutation with the subject line beneath, then the body divided into introduction, details and conclusion bands, and finally the subscription with the signature. Arrows down the left margin mark the direction the reader moves through the parts.

figures.caption: Figure: formal and informal at a glance
figures.description: Two parallel columns headed Formal and Informal, each with four rows aligned across: purpose (a request to an office versus news to a person), opening (subject line and statement versus greeting and remark), body (ordered details with dates versus incidents and enquiries), and close (Yours faithfully versus Yours affectionately). A centre line between the columns marks what changes, while the identical row structure shows that the frame itself does not.

keyPoints: The syllabus records one letter from a choice of two subjects, with suggestions possibly provided.
Address, introduction, conclusion and layout are the elements named as assessed — the frame of the letter, not its style.
No letter subjects are prescribed; the reusable content of this task is the format itself.
The formal letter states its purpose in the subject line and first sentence and holds a polite, brief register throughout.
The informal letter changes the register, not the structure: address, date, purpose, development and close are all still present.
The subscription must match the relationship — a formal formula to an office, a warm one to a friend.
The body develops the purpose in three moves: introduction, ordered details, courteous conclusion.
The subject line belongs between the salutation and the opening paragraph of a formal letter, and has no place in an informal one.
Layout faults are the cheapest to fix and the most visible to check, because the last read can catch all of them at once.
examFocus: Begin the formal body with the purpose; if the subject line carries it, the first sentence must repeat it as a complete statement.
Choose between the two subjects by content, not difficulty — the format is identical and familiarity with the material decides it.
Keep every paragraph of the body tied to the purpose: details and dates that serve the request, never background for its own sake.
Match salutation, tone and subscription to one register; a mismatch is visible to a reader before any content is judged.
Close the purpose in the final paragraph — a request repeated courteously, a thank-you, a wish — and stop there.
Check the frame last: address, date, salutation, subject, body, subscription, in order, from the recipient’s point of view.

vocabulary.meaning: Letter writing — the task of composing a letter in a set format.
vocabulary.context: Patra lekhan is one of the tasks the syllabus lists for Section A.

vocabulary.meaning: The subject line naming the purpose of a formal letter.
vocabulary.context: The vishay sits between the salutation and the opening paragraph.

vocabulary.meaning: The salutation or form of address with which the body opens.
vocabulary.context: A formal sambodhan respects the office; an informal one uses the person’s name.

vocabulary.meaning: The subscription: the closing formula and signature of a letter.
vocabulary.context: The samapan must match the relationship the rest of the letter has established.

vocabulary.meaning: The purpose — what the letter is being written to achieve.
vocabulary.context: State the uddeshya in the introduction and repeat it in the conclusion.

vocabulary.meaning: Style or manner of writing — the register a letter holds.
vocabulary.context: A formal andaz and an informal andaz differ in tone, not in structure.

vocabulary.meaning: Formal — in accordance with form and office.
vocabulary.context: A vidhivat letter to an official ends with a formal subscription.

vocabulary.meaning: A respectful greeting or salutation written at the start of a letter.
vocabulary.context: The abhivadan sets the register before the first sentence of the body is read.

vocabulary.meaning: An informal note or letter — the register of personal correspondence.
vocabulary.context: A chitthi to a friend may be warm, but it still carries address, date and close.

questions.prompt: What does the syllabus statement recorded for this subject say about the choice of letter subject?
options: One letter from a choice of two subjects
Two letters, both on prescribed topics
One letter from a fixed prescribed subject
A letter and a separate application
questions.answer: One letter from a choice of two subjects
questions.explanation: The statement records a single letter written from a choice of two subjects, with suggestions possibly provided. The task therefore rewards practising the format until any subject can be handled, rather than memorising topics.
questions.commonMistake: Preparing for two letters because two subjects are offered — the choice means you write one, not both.

questions.prompt: Which set does the syllabus statement name as assessed in the letter?
options: Number of paragraphs and vocabulary range
questions.explanation: The statement names the frame of the letter rather than its style: where it comes from and goes to, how it begins, how it ends, and how the parts are arranged. The other options are not recorded anywhere in the task.
questions.commonMistake: Polishing vocabulary and length while the actual assessed elements — the frame — are left unordered.

questions.prompt: The complimentary close “Yours faithfully” belongs to which kind of letter?
options: A formal letter to an official or institution
An informal letter to a friend
A letter to a close relative
questions.answer: A formal letter to an official or institution
questions.explanation: The close must match the relationship: formal letters to offices and officials end with a formal formula such as Yours faithfully, while letters to friends and relatives end warmly. Mixing them contradicts the register the body has held.
questions.commonMistake: Using one closing formula for every letter — the subscription is part of the register, not a formality appended at the end.

questions.prompt: Where does the subject line belong in a formal letter?
options: Between the salutation and the opening paragraph
At the end of the letter, before the signature
questions.answer: Between the salutation and the opening paragraph
questions.explanation: The subject line sits after the salutation and before the body so the reader knows the purpose before reading the details. An informal letter has no subject line at all, because its opening paragraph performs that job.
questions.commonMistake: Placing the subject above the salutation or leaving it out entirely, both of which make the reader hunt for the purpose.

questions.prompt: Complete: the closing part of a letter is called the ________ , and in a formal letter it is a formula such as ________ .
questions.explanation: The subscription is the closing unit of the letter — the leave-taking formula with the signature below it. Formal letters use a formula matched to the addressee, and informal letters use a warm one such as Yours affectionately.
questions.commonMistake: Writing “Yours lovingly” in a formal application, or “Yours faithfully” to a friend — the close must match the relationship.

questions.prompt: The syllabus allows a choice of two letter subjects. How should you choose between them when the paper is in front of you?
questions.answer: Choose the subject whose purpose you can develop most fully. Read both, and decide which one gives you three clear units of content — the reason for writing, the details or request, and the courteous close — then commit to it. If both are workable, take the one whose situation you have practised more often, because the assessed frame is identical either way and familiarity saves minutes for the final check.
questions.explanation: The choice is about content, not difficulty: the format does not change between the subjects, so the only real difference is how much you have to say. Choosing by content removes the risk of a full page with nothing developed in it.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the subject with the shorter words, then finding there is too little to develop across three paragraphs.

questions.prompt: What must the introduction of a letter accomplish?
questions.answer: It must state the purpose early and completely: within the first two or three sentences the reader should know who is writing, why, and what is being asked or said — a request visible as a request, news visible as news. Everything after it develops that purpose, and the conclusion closes it politely instead of introducing a new point.
questions.explanation: The introduction is one of the elements the syllabus statement names as assessed, and its job is orientation: a reader who must hunt for the purpose has already lost the efficiency a letter exists to provide.
questions.commonMistake: Opening with weather, health or general remarks in a formal letter, so that the purpose arrives in the second paragraph.

questions.prompt: Write out the layout of a formal letter in order and explain the job each part does.
questions.answer: 1. Sender’s address — tells the reader where the letter comes from and where a reply can go. 2. Date — fixes when it was written, which matters for any request with a deadline. 3. Receiver’s address and salutation — identifies the person or office addressed and opens with the respect the relationship requires. 4. Subject line — names the purpose in one line so the letter is read and filed correctly. 5. Introduction paragraph — who is writing and why, stated completely. 6. Middle paragraphs — the details, request or information, one point per paragraph, with dates and numbers made precise. 7. Final paragraph — the courteous close that repeats the purpose as a request or thanks. 8. Subscription and signature — the formal leave-taking with the writer’s name below it. Each part has one job, and the order as a whole is what the syllabus statement means when it lists layout among the assessed elements.
questions.explanation: The order is the answer: a letter is a frame the reader navigates, so giving the parts in sequence with the function of each shows the frame can be built from memory. The closing sentence ties the layout back to the syllabus wording, which turns a list into an answer about the task.
questions.commonMistake: Beginning the body at the top of the page and attaching the address afterwards, which removes the reader-oriented frame the layout exists to provide.

questions.prompt: Contrast a formal and an informal letter under tone, opening, body and close, giving an original opening line for each.
questions.answer: Tone: formal is polite, brief and businesslike; informal is warm, personal and conversational. Opening: the formal letter opens with address, salutation and subject and then states its purpose in the first sentence; the informal letter opens with a greeting and a natural first remark about the person or occasion. Body: the formal body develops the request or information in ordered paragraphs with precise dates and facts; the informal body moves through news, feelings and enquiries in the order the relationship takes them. Close: the formal letter ends with Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely before the signature; the informal one ends with Yours affectionately or Yours lovingly. Original formal opening: “I am writing to request three days’ leave from 14 October, as my sister’s wedding keeps me away from school.” Original informal opening: “It has been a month since we last met, and the terrace where we used to study has been waiting for you.”
questions.explanation: Contrast answers earn their marks from parallel structure — the same four headings for both letters — plus openings that actually demonstrate the tone difference instead of describing it. Both model openings here are original and specific, which is what a model must be.
questions.commonMistake: Calling informal letters casual and dropping the conclusion; warmth is not the same as shapelessness, and the informal letter still needs a close that completes it.

questions.prompt: A student writes to the Principal beginning “Dear Sir, hope you are fine. Today I am writing because I want leave...” with no subject line. Identify the faults and rewrite the beginning.
questions.answer: The faults are three. The first sentence wastes itself on a pleasantry that belongs to an informal letter, so the purpose — what the reader needs — arrives second; the tone is chatty where a formal register is expected; and the subject line, which should name the purpose before the body begins, is missing altogether. Rewritten beginning: “Ridhi Sharma, Class IX-B. Subject: Application for three days’ leave, 14 to 16 October. Respected Sir, I write to request three days’ leave from 14 to 16 October, as my sister’s wedding requires me to be away from school. I will complete the assigned work before I leave.” The rewrite states the purpose in the subject line and the first sentence, keeps the register formal throughout, and gives the dates precisely so the request can be acted on without a reply asking for them.
questions.explanation: A comment question wants fault, effect and correction for each fault: name the informality, say what it costs the reader, and show the fix in the rewrite. The rewritten opening is the evidence that the faults were understood rather than merely listed.
questions.commonMistake: Adding only a subject line and leaving the chatty opening untouched, when the register of the first sentence is the larger fault.
